Article: Leaked LiteLLM Master Key Let Attackers Steal GitHub Tokens and Hijack Release Pipeline
https://thehackernews.com/2026/10/leaked-litellm-master-key-let-attackers.html
Feed: 4228, 2026-10-24

Evidence root:
/usr/local/var/cyclotron/tmp.noindex/cyclotron-28a4cdc2/scratch/threat-feed/4228

The saved article.txt ends mid-sentence. Forager recovered the full HTML into
research/generic/. The extracted text, outbound links, three original images,
and an empty code-block extraction are under research/. The article has no
inline pre/code blocks. The configuration screenshot shows the accidental
key exposure; it is context, not a malicious specimen. The execution diagram
shows Python startup hooks, encrypted collection and an optional remote loader.

Primary linked technical sources consulted:
https://docs.litellm.ai/blog/security-incident-oct-21-2026-attack-chain
https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/issues/47826

https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/10/23/inside-the-litellm-1-107-0-supply-chain-compromise-credential-theft-through-python-startup-hooks/
The linked Socket blog rejected access (Forager cannot handle blog URLs for
that provider, ordinary HTTP returned 403). The vendor and original commits
supply the workflow evidence independently.

Recovery, all with Forager:
- pkg:pypi/litellm@1.107.0 --all-wheels: PyPI JSON 404; browser fallback
  unavailable (Chromium ICU initialization failed).
- The macOS x86-64 wheel hash was unavailable through MalwareBazaar, Triage
  and Malshare. No wheel archive was reconstructed or substituted as original.
- Workflow from b69bc36/.github/workflows/cache.yml: original bytes recovered.
- Workflow from 1a6e3c1/.github/workflows/cache.yml: original bytes recovered.
- cook/purelib/cook.py and cook/purelib/sitecustomize.py from fork commit
  20535d8f: original source bytes recovered through the BerriAI repository's
  shared fork object namespace. Hashes verified against the technical reports.
- Initial attempts at repository-root cook.py/sitecustomize.py failed; the
  original issue identifies the correct cook/purelib/ paths.

Rule changes:
Later review: the counted shell write rule was relocated to the neutral
micro-behaviors/fs/write/credential::shell-multiple-credential-variable-writes.
Its matcher and count are unchanged; multiple static sites can provision a
single token through mutually exclusive branches. Encoded-upload coverage is
retained. See testdata/version-drift-renovate/evidence.md for the release diff,
consumer audit and original-workflow regression results.

- Parsed shell writes require a quoted variable expansion, a credential label
  ending TOKEN/KEY/PASSWORD, and a real file redirect. Multiple such writes
  establish suspicious plaintext credential staging. Neither alias names nor
  package/repository names are required.
- Parsed Base64 command output redirection fills the direct-file encoding gap
  left by the existing pipe-to-base64 matcher. Decode options do not qualify.
- Suspicious encoded-upload composite requires the credential staging, encoder
  output and a real curl file-body upload in one shell unit. It deliberately
  describes co-occurrence: it does not bind the staged and uploaded filenames.
- Shared shell mechanisms cover Unix and Windows bash runners. Controls vary
  aliases, filenames, receiver, echo/printf and GNU/BSD Base64 syntax. Existing
  Python traits cover the recovered credential collector and startup backdoor.
- Removed objectives/supply-chain/recon-exfil/secrets::webhook-site-token:
  its matcher was neutral callback-path recognition in an intent namespace.
  Reused micro-behaviors/communications/http/url/endpoint::webhook-site-uuid-path
  and added github-actions to its formats. Removed its unsupported T1041 mapping.
  The broader arbitrary 12-character token form is intentionally no longer a
  collector assertion; the canonical rule recognizes the provider's UUID paths.
  The exact consumer and the one source-directory consumer were updated. Other
  source rules remain unchanged. No whole-destination selector was introduced.

Verification:
- cleave facts on the original workflow and both Python files, including their
  decoded strings; preserved under research/.
- check.py generates focused positive/negative controls in cleave's fixtures,
  outside the feed sample set. It checks all new findings and callback reuse.
- Original-sample floor results and exact hostile/suspicious IDs are recorded
  by research/detection-floors.json and research/atomscan-final.json.
- Required final check: make validate.

Indicator scope:
testdata/SHA256 contains the reported malicious wheel/startup/decoded hashes,
the tampered 1.107.0 sdist hash, and computed hashes of the two recovered
workflows. The sdist has tampered maturin data configuration, not the payload
files. Git commit IDs and clean comparison hashes are excluded.
testdata/PURLS records PyPI 1.107.0 and the specifically named Docker Hub/GHCR
channels/tags. The mutable container coordinates describe the incident window
on October 21 (Docker Hub 11:46:56--14:20 UTC; GHCR unavailable by 13:51 UTC),
not the contents of those tags after removal/repointing. Clean comparison
versions and unrelated LiteLLM packages are excluded. No version is inferred.
testdata/ENDPOINTS records the two attacker-origin IPs, the exfiltration domain
and www variant, and webhook.site. The shared webhook host is suspicious only
with its two cited UUID paths, not every user's endpoint. The shared raw GitHub
host is not a malicious identity: the precise dead-drop URL is
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/letters9813/pythonclient-test/main/domain.txt
and the next-stage path is http://{returned-domain}/codepy.
The credential-export path is http://www.litellm.dev/healthcheck.

Limits:
Static code cannot establish which stolen token actually approved a release,
whether branch protections were bypassed, or whether run logs were deleted;
those claims require GitHub audit evidence. No static traits were invented for
those events. The optional remote second stage was not confirmed downloaded or
executed by researchers. Flow analysis reports limitations in the large Python
collector, and shell file identity is not proven by the new co-occurrence rule.
